name: gzrt
why: Recovers data from corrupted gzip archives by scanning deflate streams, a good window into how compressed formats actually break.

brief.what_it_is: gzrecover is a command-line program from the gzip Recovery Toolkit (gzrt) that tries to salvage data from a corrupted .gz file. It reads a damaged gzip archive, either from a named file or from standard input, and skips over bad bytes. It writes whatever it can read to a new file named with a .recovered suffix (any .gz is stripped), or to standard output with -p. The output is not guaranteed to be good, so the author says it must be checked by hand.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wrote it after a backup restore failed: bad sectors had corrupted the archive, and gzip stopped about 10% of the way through, so almost everything was lost. The README's framing is that gzip 'craps out' on the first error, and gzrecover is meant to get past bad data and keep what it can.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the internal algorithm. It says gzrecover 'attempts to skip over bad data in a gzip archive', that it reports where it finds bad bytes when run with -v, and that it runs slower than gunzip, more so the more corrupt the file. It does not say it scans deflate streams, so that detail comes from the scout note and is unverified here. For tarballs, the workflow is to run gzrecover first and then pass the .recovered output to GNU cpio, since GNU tar cannot handle format errors.

commands_seen.context: Builds the gzrecover program from the unpacked gzrt source directory. The README says to install by copying the binary manually to a directory of your choice.
Suggested way to check whether GNU cpio is installed and at version 2.6 or higher, which is needed only for recovering compressed tar files.
Runs recovery on a corrupted gzipped tarball. Per the README's example, it writes my-corrupted-backup.tar.recovered alongside the input.
Extracts files from the recovered tar stream with GNU cpio, which tolerates format errors that GNU tar rejects. The README's example uses this after gzrecover.

brief.install_notes: You need zlib, which you may already have; build and install it first if not. Unpack the gzrt sources, cd into the gzrt directory, and run make. There is no make install step: the README says to copy the binary manually to a directory of your choice. For compressed tar archives you also need GNU cpio 2.6 or higher, which the README says is only needed if you don't already have it. The README mentions a 0.8 release (2013-10-03) and a GitHub repository, but the GitHub link's URL was not given on the homepage, so I did not follow it. The brew formula's executable is gzrecover.
brief.standout: Rather than trying to decompress the whole stream, it treats a corrupt gzip file as something to scan past its damage and keep what can be read. It pairs with cpio for tarballs because cpio tolerates errors that tar does not, which is a practical recovery chain for backups.
brief.status: quiet. The latest release listed is 0.8, dated 2013-10-03, and the copyright line runs 2002-2013. The page shows no commits or releases after that, and I did not check the GitHub repository's activity.
brief.caveats: Output is not guaranteed to be valid and the author warns it 'is likely to recover some bad data', so everything must be checked by hand; the bigger the file, the more likely it extracts something. Runtime grows with corruption and can be long, and cpio can produce very verbose errors and run for a long time. The README gives no platform list; the build is a plain make with zlib, and the docs assume a Unix-style shell. The program is GPL-licensed, but the copyright notice also says 'All Rights Reserved' under a separate line. Also, before recovering, check that the file was not transferred by FTP in ASCII mode, which the author says causes 99% of corruption reports.
quotes: gzip craps out 10% of the way through your archive.
99% of "corrupted" gzip archives are caused by transferring the file via FTP in ASCII mode instead of binary mode.
This program is provided AS IS with absolutely NO WARRANTY.
fetch_log: https://www.urbanophile.com/arenn/coding/gzrt/gzrt.html: loaded OK; README-style page with usage, install steps, and an example. Did not follow the GitHub repository link, since its URL was not given, and did not fetch the ChangeLog, which was not linked.

judge.reason: This obscure tool attempts to skip damage in a gzip stream and salvage later data, making compression recovery an unusual, practical thing to explore.

entry.title: gzrt
entry.tldr: gzrecover skips past the damaged bytes in a corrupted .gz file and saves whatever it can still read, where gunzip gives up at the first error.
entry.deeper_look:
gzrecover is the one program in the gzip Recovery Toolkit. It reads a damaged gzip archive, from a file or from standard input, and skips over bad data. What it manages to read goes into a new file with a `.recovered` suffix (any `.gz` is stripped), or to standard output with `-p`. Run with `-v`, it reports where it found bad bytes.

The author wrote it after a backup restore failed. Bad sectors had corrupted the archive, and gzip stopped about 10% of the way through. In the README's words, "gzip craps out 10% of the way through your archive." Most of the backup was lost, and gzrecover is the attempt to get the rest back. The README does not describe the internal algorithm. A scout note says it scans deflate streams, but that is not confirmed by the README.

The idea underneath is that a compressed file is a chain of dependent pieces, so one flipped bit can wreck everything after it for a normal decompressor. A tool that tolerates the damage and keeps going shows how those formats fail and how much is still recoverable.

For tarballs there is a two-step chain. Run gzrecover first, then hand the `.recovered` file to GNU cpio, because GNU tar rejects format errors that cpio tolerates.

The output is not guaranteed to be good. The README says plainly that "Everything should be manually verified."
entry.install:
brew install gzrt
# installs the gzrecover executable
# for recovered tarballs, GNU cpio 2.6 or higher is also needed

try_this.what_happens: Scans the damaged archive and writes whatever it can read to my-corrupted-backup.tar.recovered next to the input.
Extracts files from the recovered tar stream with GNU cpio, which tolerates format errors that GNU tar rejects.
Checks that GNU cpio is installed and at version 2.6 or higher, which the tarball workflow needs.

entry.whats_unique: Instead of giving up at the first error like gunzip, it skips past the damage and keeps whatever it can read. It pairs with cpio for tarballs, which gives a practical recovery chain for broken backups.
entry.caveats: The latest release is 0.8 from 2013, and the author warns the output is likely to include some bad data, so everything must be checked by hand; it also gets slower the more corrupt the file is.
